audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 1 Samuel / Shemuel Aleph chapter 31, draft aligned later
audit_status.review_note: First-pass draft reviewed for Gilboa battle, deaths of Saul's sons, Saul's wound and fear of abuse, armor-bearer's refusal, self-inflicted deaths, civilian flight, stripping and beheading, temple display, Beth-shan exposure, Jabesh-gilead recovery, burning, burial, and seven-day fast.

verses.restored: Philistines were fighting against Israel. Men of Israel fled from before Philistines and fell slain on mount Gilboa.

familiar.text: Now the Philistines fought against Israel: and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines, and fell down slain in mount Gilboa.

modern.text: Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before them, and many fell slain on Mount Gilboa.

original.text: וּפְלִשְׁתִּ֖ים נִלְחָמִ֣ים בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיָּנֻ֜סוּ אַנְשֵׁ֤י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מִפְּנֵ֣י פְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וַיִּפְּל֥וּ חֲלָלִ֖ים בְּהַ֥ר הַגִּלְבֹּֽעַ

verses.restored: Philistines clung closely to Saul and to his sons. Philistines struck Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua, sons of Saul.

familiar.text: And the Philistines followed hard upon Saul and upon his sons; and the Philistines slew Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Melchishua, Saul’s sons.

modern.text: The Philistines followed hard after Saul and his sons, and they killed Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua.

verses.restored: Battle was heavy against Saul. Shooters, men with bow, found him, and he trembled/writhed greatly because of shooters.

familiar.text: And the battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him; and he was sore wounded of the archers.

modern.text: When the battle intensified against Saul, the archers overtook him and wounded him critically.

original.text: וַתִּכְבַּ֤ד הַמִּלְחָמָה֙ אֶל שָׁא֔וּל וַיִּמְצָאֻ֥הוּ הַמּוֹרִ֖ים אֲנָשִׁ֣ים בַּקָּ֑שֶׁת וַיָּ֥חֶל מְאֹ֖ד מֵהַמּוֹרִֽים

verses.restored: Saul said to bearer of his weapons, Draw your sword and pierce me with it, lest these uncircumcised come and pierce me and abuse/make sport of me. But bearer of his weapons was not willing, because he was greatly afraid. Saul took sword and fell upon it.

familiar.text: Then said Saul unto his armourbearer, Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and abuse me. But his armourbearer would not; for he was sore afraid. Therefore Saul took a sword, and fell upon it.

modern.text: Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and run it through me, or these uncircumcised men will come and run me through and torture me!” But his armor-bearer was terrified and refused to do it. So Saul took his own sword and fell on it.

familiar.text: And when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise upon his sword, and died with him.

modern.text: When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell on his own sword and died with him.

modern.text: So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that same day. The Philistines Possess the Towns (1 Chronicles 10:7–10)

verses.restored: Men of Israel who were across valley and who were across Jordan saw that men of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons had died. They abandoned cities and fled, and Philistines came and lived in them.

familiar.text: And when the men of Israel that were on the other side of the valley, and they that were on the other side Jordan, saw that the men of Israel fled, and that Saul and his sons were dead, they forsook the cities, and fled; and the Philistines came and dwelt in them.

modern.text: When the Israelites along the valley and those on the other side of the Jordan saw that the army of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons had died, they abandoned their cities and ran away. So the Philistines came and occupied their cities.

verses.restored: On next day, Philistines came to strip slain, and they found Saul and his three sons fallen on mount Gilboa.

familiar.text: And it came to pass on the morrow, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, that they found Saul and his three sons fallen in mount Gilboa.

modern.text: The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the dead, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.

verses.restored: They cut off his head and stripped his weapons. They sent through land of Philistines all around, to announce good news in house of their idols and among people.

familiar.text: And they cut off his head, and stripped off his armour, and sent into the land of the Philistines round about, to publish it in the house of their idols, and among the people.

modern.text: They cut off Saul’s head, stripped off his armor, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to proclaim the news in the temples of their idols and among their people.

translation_notes: Saul's death occurs under battlefield injury, terror of torture, and collapse of his army. It must never be romanticized as noble suicide, prescribed as a response to shame, or used to condemn people who die by suicide.
The armor-bearer's refusal to kill Saul is valid. A subordinate is not obligated to perform assisted death, and his own subsequent death is tragedy, not loyalty's highest form.
The phrase about 'uncircumcised' enemies is ancient ethnic-religious contempt spoken in fear. It may not authorize antisemitism, anti-Philistine hatred, genital shaming, or modern ethnic slurs.
Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua have distinct lives; they should not disappear into Saul's downfall. Jonathan's death particularly closes a relationship of covenant love with David.
Philistine stripping, beheading, display, and temple placement are corpse desecration and war propaganda. They are not harmless celebration or permission to humiliate enemy dead.
Flight from abandoned cities foregrounds civilians displaced by regime collapse and war. Territorial transfer is not a clean military statistic.
Jabesh-gilead's recovery of the bodies repays remembered solidarity from chapter 11. Burial and fasting restore dignity without erasing Saul's harms.
Burning the bodies here is a context-specific mortuary response, not evidence that cremation is shameful or forbidden.
The chapter's ending is lament. Royal failure, military defeat, suicide, and public desecration should never become spectacle.
safety_note: Maximum suicide-misuse safeguards: Do not praise, imitate, spiritualize, or prescribe Saul's or the armor-bearer's deaths. Do not shame survivors, people with suicidal thoughts, or families bereaved by suicide. The narrative depicts injury, fear, coercive honor, and catastrophic loss. Center prevention, care, dignity of the dead, civilian displacement, and communal mourning.
